title: ERNet: Unsupervised Collective Extraction and Registration in Neuroimaging Data

problem.claim: Brain extraction and registration must be performed on neuroimaging data, but collecting voxel-level labels and conducting manual quality control are expensive and time-consuming.

gap.claim: Existing research mainly addresses extraction and registration separately under supervised settings, despite the tasks being highly related and suitable for collective solution.

contributions.claim: ERNet is a unified end-to-end framework for unsupervised collective extraction and registration that jointly optimizes both tasks and allows feedback between them.

The framework uses paired multi-stage extraction and registration modules to learn an extraction mask and transformation, incrementally improving extraction and successively warping the extracted image toward alignment with a target image.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets show that the proposed method can effectively improve performance on neuroimaging extraction and registration tasks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Brain extraction and registration are important neuroimaging preprocessing tasks involving brain-region extraction and alignment to a target image.
Conventional supervised methods address the tasks separately and depend on training samples and expert visual inspection, while labels and manual quality control are costly.
Because extraction and registration are highly related, the paper studies solving them collectively without supervision.
ERNet jointly optimizes extraction and registration through feedback between multi-stage extraction and registration modules.
The authors report improved extraction and registration performance on real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: The extraction and registration modules are jointly optimized and provide feedback to each other.

interpretation.claim: When related preprocessing tasks influence one another, a coupled model may address limitations caused by optimizing them independently.

application.claim: Consider jointly modeling dependent preprocessing stages when their intermediate outputs can provide useful feedback.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that joint optimization is preferable for unrelated tasks or across settings beyond the reported neuroimaging experiments.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the real-world datasets, evaluation metrics, baseline methods, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not describe the unsupervised training objective or implementation details.
